Quantile grid for the mean scan

Source: R/quantile_grid.R
quantile_grid.Rd

quantile_grid() produces the \(n \times K\) matrix of conditional quantiles of \(Y\) given \(R = 1, X = x_i\) at the levels \((k - 1/2)/K\) that sharp_scan_mean() takes as q. It is a convenience like scan_inputs(), not a commitment to a learner, and accepts three kinds of fit:

Usage

quantile_grid(fit, newdata = NULL, K = 200L)

Arguments

fit

An rq/rqs object, a function(tau, newdata), or a numeric matrix of draws.

newdata

Rows at which the quantiles are wanted (for rq and function fits).

K

Number of levels. Default 200.

Value

A numeric matrix, nrow(newdata) (or nrow(fit) for draws) by K, rows sorted, with attributes "levels", "crossing" and "shift".

Details

  • a quantile regression from quantreg (rq or rqs), fitted on the observed rows. It is refitted at the K levels with update(), so the data it was fitted on must still be reachable, and predicted at newdata;

  • a function function(tau, newdata) returning, for a vector of levels tau, a matrix with one row per row of newdata and one column per level – for any other conditional quantile model;

  • a numeric matrix of draws from the conditional distribution, one row per row of interest and any number of draws per row – for a distributional or generative model. newdata is then not used.

Quantile curves estimated level by level can cross. Each row is sorted (rearranged), which yields a proper quantile function and never moves it further from the truth (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val and Galichon, 2010). With many levels nearly every row crosses somewhere by sampling noise alone, so the share of rows that needed it (attribute "crossing") says little. Attribute "shift" says how much was moved: the median over rows of the largest change by sorting, relative to the row's range. A few percent is noise; a large shift says the quantile model is poor.

References

Chernozhukov, V., Fernández-Val, I. and Galichon, A. (2010). Quantile and probability curves without crossing. Econometrica, 78(3), 1093–1125. doi:10.3982/ECTA7880

See also

sharp_scan_mean()

Examples

dc <- simulate_shadow(3000, tilt = -1, outcome = "continuous", seed = 1)
obs <- dc[dc$observed == 1, ]
rej <- dc[dc$observed == 0, ]
# any conditional quantile model, here a location model fitted by lm()
m <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + z_shadow + z_policy + z_score, data = obs)
res <- residuals(m)
q <- quantile_grid(function(tau, newdata)
  outer(predict(m, newdata), quantile(res, tau, names = FALSE), "+"),
  rej, K = 100)
sm <- sharp_scan_mean(q, rej$obs_rate, threshold = 0.5)
sm
#> <sharp_scan_mean> sharp identified set for a mean under a propensity ratio <= exp(lambda)
#>   rows: 1803   aggregation: union 
#>   lambda = 0 (model on observed rows): -0.0117 
#>   lambda = 2 (propensity ratio 7.39): sharp [-0.718, 0.762], outer [-0.741, 0.775]
#>   threshold 0.5 reached by
#>     sharp set:   lambda = 1.31 (propensity ratio 3.71) 
#>     outer band:  lambda = 1.31 (propensity ratio 3.71) 
if (requireNamespace("quantreg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fq <- quantreg::rq(y ~ x1 + x2 + z_shadow + z_policy + z_score,
                     tau = 0.5, data = obs)
  q2 <- quantile_grid(fq, rej, K = 50)
  attr(q2, "crossing")
}
#> [1] 0.452579
